selected.name: Conversational Deadpan Delivery
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption mimics a completely mundane, casual remark or complaint that sharply contrasts with the absolute chaos or surrealism of the drawing; score 0 if the tone is melodramatic, exclamatory, or explicitly acknowledges the weirdness.
selected.rationale: The juxtaposition of a casual tone with a chaotic scene is a classic contest technique. R10 ('he got indicted') and R46 ('you're rambling again') rank incredibly high for the dense model because they treat the surreal parade with deadpan casualness, a nuance the scorecard appears to miss.

selected.name: Two-reading semantic fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when one phrase supports both a literal reading and an idiomatic or conceptual reading, with both fitting the cartoon; score 0 when only one unforced meaning is present.
selected.rationale: Rows R04, R06, and R23 use “cross word,” “keys,” or “gravity” so the wording operates simultaneously in the caption and the image.

selected.name: Phonetic pun precision
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound-alike or word-form substitution is exact, immediately decipherable, and image-specific; score 0 when the pun is strained, obscure, or detachable from the cartoon.
selected.rationale: Rows R24, R39, and R49 demonstrate compact sound or spelling transformations tied to piano, bird, and sheep imagery.

selected.name: Pun anchored in vocabulary the scene already requires
selected.instruction: Score whether wordplay is built from a word the scene forces into the sentence anyway, versus a word imported to enable the pun. 10 = the pivot word is one the speaker would naturally use in this situation, and its second meaning arrives as a bonus. 5 = the pun word fits but had to be steered toward. 0 = the sentence is visibly bent, or an unrelated object introduced, so the pun can happen.
selected.rationale: R37 ('88 keys and no locks') and R23 ('it's so ewe') and R35 ('i love that it's 100 wool') use words the scene already demands (piano keys, sheep, wool) and are dense-high. R28 ('the only house i could find under a grand') and R05 ('that's a blues jay') import the pun and are dense-low despite card scores of 0.607 and 0.779, indicating the bank likely rewards pun presence without testing anchoring.
member_names: Dual-anchor pun: specific object plus idiom
Pun anchored in vocabulary the scene already requires

selected.name: Cultural allusion payoff
selected.instruction: Give 10 when a recognizable song, person, institution, or established phrase adds a second layer directly illuminating the cartoon; give 0 when the reference is obscure, decorative, or removable without loss.
selected.rationale: R20 invokes Watson while preserving the crossword premise, R46 invokes a recognizable political institution through the costume display, and R52 converts extinction into a band reference. Each allusion contributes interpretive work.

selected.name: Cynical or Legalistic Anthropomorphism
selected.instruction: Score 10 if an animal or inanimate object is given a highly specific, jaded, legalistic, or bureaucratic human motivation that perfectly clashes with its nature; score 0 if the animal is just given a generic, cute human trait.
selected.rationale: Instead of basic anthropomorphism, the dense model rewards specific, cynical human traits. R47 ('exposed skin implies consent') and R60 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night') give jaded/human traits to a mosquito and digestive tract respectively, scoring highly for dense, while the scorecard undervalues this cynical layer.

selected.name: Delayed punchline timing
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the sentence withholds its key reinterpretive word or phrase until the end; score 0 when there is no turn or the punchline is stated before the setup can work.
selected.rationale: Rows R10, R24, and R34 reserve “under a grand,” “wreckmaninoff,” or “cover” for the final turn, creating compact verbal timing.

selected.name: Verbal throat-clearing before the joke
selected.instruction: Score the absence of scaffolding phrases that announce, cushion, or introduce the punchline. Score 10 when the caption begins in the joke, with no lead-in. Score 0 when it opens with or leans on discourse framing -- 'believe it or not', 'actually', 'guess i'll', 'i don't know about you, but', 'on the plus side', 'i can usually X, but', 'remember when' -- that tells the reader a joke is arriving instead of delivering it. Score 5 for a single light connective that also carries meaning. Judge only the framing words, not the caption's total length.
selected.rationale: R20 opens 'believe it or not', R38 opens 'actually', R14 opens 'guess i'll', R30 opens 'i don't know about you, but', R53 opens 'on the plus side', R35 opens 'i can usually... but' -- six captions in this slice that spend their opening on announcing the joke. The tightest lines in the slice (R07, R23, R29, R05) have none. Scaffolding makes a caption read as fluent, well-formed prose, which is exactly what fluency- or naturalness-shaped criteria reward.

selected.name: Domestication of the fantastic into mundane routine
selected.instruction: Score how fully the caption treats the cartoon's impossible or absurd element as an unremarkable, everyday occurrence, folding it into ordinary domestic/social logic with zero acknowledgment of its strangeness. 10 = the impossible premise is completely normalized into routine, low-stakes dialogue; 0 = the caption explicitly marks the scene as bizarre, shocking, or impossible.
selected.rationale: R58 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') treats a shopping bear's checkout visit as an ordinary parenting-white-lie moment; R12 ('i'm thinking takeout') treats a booby-trapped kitchen as just another dinner-plan decision. Both dense_low_card_high (dense .338/.155 vs card .991/.975), the two highest card_pct scores in the slice.
member_names: Domestication of the fantastic into mundane routine

selected.name: Role-specific voice
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds like a plausible utterance from the depicted speaker and reflects that speaker’s role, relationship, or species; score 0 when it sounds like detached narration.
selected.rationale: Rows R02, R27, and R35 use the perspectives of a Reaper, a dog trainer, and a bear parent to shape the line.

selected.name: Layered/compound wordplay stacking multiple puns
selected.instruction: Score how many independent puns, double meanings, or wordplay devices are stacked within the single caption so they mutually reinforce one joke. 10 = two or more distinct wordplay mechanisms compound in one short line; 5 = exactly one clean pun with no stacking; 0 = no wordplay present.
selected.rationale: R06 ('wreckmaninoff') fuses 'wreck' with the composer Rachmaninoff, simultaneously invoking the piano, the destruction, and classical-music snobbery in one coined word; R46 ('now the house has 88 keys and no locks') stacks the piano-keys pun with a literal 'keys and locks' security pun. Both are dense_high_card_low (dense .794/.714 vs card .164/.117), suggesting the scorecard undercredits compounded wordplay relative to simpler entries.

selected.name: Sound-pun aimed at the scene's central absurdity
selected.instruction: For captions whose humor is phonetic (a homophone, near-homophone, portmanteau, or respelling), score whether the transformed word names the thing that makes the drawing strange, rather than an incidental detail. Score 10 when the sound-play lands squarely on the central incongruity, so the pun and the premise are the same object. Score 5 when it lands on a real element of the scene that is not the source of the strangeness. Score 0 when the phonetic play is on a peripheral or merely adjacent detail, or when it is a sound joke with no anchor in the picture at all. Captions with no phonetic play should be scored 0 on this axis without prejudice.
selected.rationale: R07 ('it's so ewe') puts the pun exactly on the sheep-disguise premise, and R23 ('wreckmaninoff') fuses the wreck and the piano into one word. R55 ('that's a blues jay') and R52 ('a hole-in-the-wall place you'll love') are competent phonetic puns aimed at the bird's species and the mouse's habitat -- true details, but not the source of the incongruity, which is the guitar and the lab coat respectively. A bank that scores 'contains a pun' or 'wordplay quality' will rate all four similarly.
member_names: Sound-pun aimed at the scene's central absurdity

selected.name: Late-caption reveal that recontextualizes the whole line
selected.instruction: Score how much the caption withholds its point until the final word(s), forcing a re-reading of everything preceding it once the payoff lands. 10 = a strong late pivot that recasts the entire preceding clause in a new light; 0 = the caption states its point immediately with no structural delay or reversal.
selected.rationale: R48 ('there never was an engagement ring, was there') builds a neutral question that only reveals its accusatory sting on the final clause; R39 ('they're still looking for votes') reframes an innocuous couch scene only once 'votes' recontextualizes the search as electoral. Both dense_high_card_low (dense .836/.970 vs card .338/.085).
member_names: Late-caption reveal that recontextualizes the whole line

selected.name: Caption voiced from the anomalous/nonhuman character's POV
selected.instruction: Score how clearly the caption is spoken in-character as the cartoon's impossible or anomalous figure (the animal, monster, or fantastical element) rather than by a neutral human bystander. 10 = caption is unambiguously voiced by the anomalous character with coherent internal logic from that perspective; 0 = caption is voiced by an unremarked outside observer commenting on the anomaly.
selected.rationale: R58 ('my cubs still think i catch my own salmon') is spoken as the shopping bear itself; R44 ('do you think it makes my teeth look big') is spoken as the wolf trying on the sheep costume; R28 ('believe it or not, they think that we look alike too') is voiced from inside the sheep/dog group. All three are dense_low_card_high (card .991/.822/.626), suggesting the scorecard rewards this perspective-taking device more than the dense model does.
member_names: Caption voiced from the anomalous/nonhuman character's POV

selected.name: Word economy
selected.instruction: Give 10 when every word advances the setup, turn, or image-specific payoff and nothing can be removed; give 0 when the caption is padded, repetitive, or diffuse.
selected.rationale: R38 compresses a damaged-house piano joke into one precise word, and R39 compresses the historical and coin meanings into five words. Their brevity increases rather than reduces interpretive density.

selected.name: Topical news and era reference
selected.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the caption explicitly references a specific contemporary political event, public figure, or cultural news item (e.g., elections, pandemics, indictments) that dates it to a particular week's news cycle. Do not judge the funniness of the reference.
selected.rationale: References like 'he got indicted' (R26), 'republican primary ticket' (R11), and 'herd immunity' (R34) date the entry to a specific era, which models might key on for general relevance without reflecting timeless caption quality.

selected.name: Obvious Idiom Taken Literally
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the caption's primary joke mechanism is applying a common idiom or cliché literally to the visual elements of the drawing (e.g., 'cross word', 'pull the wool'). The judge must not judge whether the feature is good.
selected.rationale: Idioms are the easiest, most generic prior for a cartoon. Entries like R58 ('never had a cross word') and R17 ('pull the wool over my eyes') rely on this structural shortcut. A text-only model may score these highly because they perfectly map text to the image, but editors often reject them as uncreative first-thoughts.

selected.name: Transcription and typography conventions of the compiled list
selected.instruction: MODE 4 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how much NON-DEFAULT TYPOGRAPHY the caption carries relative to the plain lowercase unpunctuated norm of this list. Add extent for: terminal punctuation present (a final period, question mark or exclamation); internal sentence-final periods splitting the line; quotation marks around an embedded phrase; double-hyphen or dash constructions; ellipses; digits written as numerals; symbols that appear stripped or mangled (a percentage or currency sign missing beside a number); any capitalisation at all. 0 = all lowercase, no terminal punctuation, no marks beyond a single comma; 10 = several of these conventions at once. You must NOT judge whether the punctuation is correct, careful or sloppy; count only how much marked typography is visible.
selected.rationale: MODE 4: whoever compiled and normalised these entries left an uneven trace, and the unevenness is legible. R58 carries both quotation marks and a terminal period ('good girl.'), R59 uses a double hyphen (no bag--my cubs), R50 reads 100 wool with the percentage sign evidently lost in transcription, R28 carries a bare numeral (581 days), R54 uses sentence-final periods for emphasis (six. feet), while the great majority of rows such as R41, R11 and R14 are bare lowercase with no terminal mark. None of this is a property of the joke's fit to the drawing, but it is trivially learnable from raw text.

selected.name: Datable era idiom fixing the entry to a period
selected.instruction: MODE 3 fingerprint. Score 0-10 for how strongly the caption's wording DATES it to a specific stretch of years, independent of any political content. Look for: pandemic-era idiom (distancing measures such as six feet, herd immunity, closures and shutdowns of restaurants or venues, masking, remote work); named consumer technology and platforms of a given moment (iphone, streaming, apps, texting); slang and address terms whose currency rises and falls (dude, hysterical); and conversely idiom that reads as older-register (telegram, party line). 0 = wording that would read the same in any decade; 5 = one mildly period-flavoured word; 10 = the caption cannot be understood without knowing what was happening in one particular year or two. You must NOT judge whether the dated reference is stale, fresh, or well used; score only how tightly the wording pins a period.
selected.rationale: MODE 3: the actual contest date is invisible, but era leaves a lexical trace. Sharp examples inside the slice: R54 (six feet dude. six. feet), R17 (they claim they have herd immunity), R12 (the worst thing to temporarily shut down a restaurant) all carry pandemic-window idiom; R06 (no tv or iphone) pins a consumer-technology era. Era membership is a property of when the entry was written, not of how well it reads its cartoon, yet it is highly visible in the tokens and therefore learnable by any text model as a shortcut.

selected.name: Generic well-formed complete-sentence 'caption-shaped' joke
selected.instruction: 0-10: how much does the caption read as a fully-formed, grammatically complete, self-contained joke sentence with a clear setup-and-punchline shape that would be recognizable as 'a good caption' even to someone who has never seen this particular drawing, versus a fragment, an oblique aside, or a line that only makes sense once you already know the specific scene? 0 = incomprehensible or meaningless without the specific drawing; 10 = polished, complete, self-contained joke sentence that reads as generically caption-shaped. Score only this generic well-formedness; do not judge whether it is actually the best caption for this drawing.
selected.rationale: R46 ('no bag--my cubs still think i catch my own salmon', dense_pct=0.338/card_pct=0.991) and R49 ('when i was a kid, we had to catch our own fish', dense_pct=0.452/card_pct=0.968) are both polished, complete, self-contained jokes that any generic reader would flag as 'a good caption,' and both are strongly card-favored while only dense-middling — showing generic well-formedness can be scored highly by a criterion bank without being what most distinguishes fit to this particular cartoon.
member_names: Generic caption-shaped joke: scaffolded setup with tidy payoff

selected.name: Terse fragment/staccato delivery
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption is delivered as short clipped fragments (very few words, punctuated as separate short bursts rather than one flowing sentence) rather than as a longer flowing sentence. 0 = long flowing single sentence with no internal breaks; 10 = extremely short, broken into staccato fragments/repeated short bursts. Score only the extent of this fragment/staccato quality present in the wording and punctuation; do not judge whether the caption is funny or good.
selected.rationale: R15 ('six feet dude. six. feet', dense_pct=0.040/card_pct=0.953) and R43 ('honey, the remote is in your hand', dense_pct=0.225/card_pct=0.947) are terse/clipped and card-favored while dense ranks them low; a longer flowing line like R37 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent', dense_pct=0.859/card_pct=0.134) is dense-favored instead — brevity/rhythm is a stylistic tell, not per-cartoon fit.

selected.name: Content outside the venue's printed register (bodily, sexual, injury, transgressive)
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the caption's content sits outside the restrained register a general-audience magazine cartoon caption normally occupies. Add extent for: sexual or anatomical reference and double entendre; scatological or excretory wording; bodily injury, mutilation or death treated as the joke's material; language about consent, coercion or violence; and any wording whose bluntness would need an editor's second look. 0 = wholly mild and printable without comment; 10 = the caption's entire payload is transgressive material. Judge ONLY how far the content sits from the mild register. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is funny, offensive, tasteful or warranted; you are measuring distance from the house register, not approving or condemning it.
selected.rationale: MODE 4 (house style) with MODE 2 structure: the unseen factor is a venue-level publication norm, and its fingerprint is the lexical register of the line. Every clearly off-register row in the slice lands dense-high and card-low: R41 ('you should see the breasts', dense_pct .929 / card_pct .042), R44 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night', .741 / .040), R26 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent', .859 / .134) and R14 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg', .656 / .076) — the four lowest card percentiles among dense-high items. A written criterion bank encodes decorum explicitly and an end-to-end reader does not, so register alone drives the gap. Whether a line is printable in a given venue is a property of the venue, not of how well the words answer that drawing, so it is a pure nuisance and must never be bankable.

selected.name: Item lacks usable cartoon context; caption reads free-standing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item, as presented, gives no drawing to read the caption against, so that the caption must be interpreted as a free-standing line. Score 10 when the cartoon field is absent, empty, or a placeholder such as '[no description available]'. Score high (7-9) when a description is present but so short or generic that it names no object, action or character the caption could hook onto. Score low (0-2) when the description names specific figures, props and the visual incongruity. Judge ONLY how much drawing-side information the item supplies. Do NOT judge whether the caption is good, and do NOT try to imagine what the missing drawing might have been.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. (a) An unseen factor beyond the caption text is whether the description generator succeeded for that cartoon. (b) Its textual fingerprint is fully visible: the '[no description available]' placeholder in the item record. (c) A judge can score the placeholder without any conjecture. Seven rows in the slice carry it and they cluster hard on one side: R08, R22, R23, R40, R42 and R48 are all dense_high_card_low (dense_pct .802, .773, .991, .827, .951, .947 against card_pct .248, .234, .474, .200, .444, .191), with only R58 on the other side. A criterion-scored rubric that must ask 'does this fit the drawing' is structurally starved on these rows while an end-to-end reader is not, so the placeholder predicts the disagreement directly. It is an artefact of corpus preparation and carries no information about entry quality; it must never be bankable.

selected.name: Word count and clause-scaffold verbosity
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual bulk in the caption only. Count the words and the number of independent or subordinate clauses, and add weight for scaffolding material that lengthens the line without adding a new referent: introductory adverbials, hedges ('i think', 'i don't know about you, but'), relative clauses, coordinated second sentences, and appositive asides. 0 = a single word or a bare noun phrase; 5 = one ordinary sentence of roughly eight to twelve words; 10 = two or more full sentences, or one sentence of twenty-plus words with several clauses. Judge LENGTH AND CLAUSE STRUCTURE ONLY. Do NOT judge whether the caption is funny, apt, well-paced, or good for the cartoon; a long caption and a short caption can both be excellent, and you are not assessing that.
selected.rationale: MODE 1. Raw token bulk tracks the split in this slice almost monotonically and independently of aptness. R23 ('you're rambling again', three words) and R38 ('wreckmaninoff', one word) sit at dense_pct .991 and .794 with card_pct .474 and .164, while R46 ('i can usually identify a bird by the song, but i think he's doing a cover') and R17 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this? it took him six days to make') are the two longest lines in the slice at dense_pct .006 and .028 against card_pct .735 and .847. R13 and R27 repeat the pattern. Length is a formatting property of the submission, not a property of how well the line answers its drawing, and a rubric that rewards elaborated criteria will absorb it mechanically; it must be discounted rather than banked.
member_names: Length, clause count and explanatory elaboration
